draft.title: Temperature and the equilibrium constant
card: The value of K for a reaction is fixed at a given temperature. Changing the temperature is the only thing that changes K.
the forward reaction releases heat. Raising the temperature lowers K, so less product is present at the new equilibrium.
the forward reaction absorbs heat. Raising the temperature raises K, so more product is present at the new equilibrium.
Changing a concentration or the pressure can move the position of equilibrium, but K stays the same. Lowering the temperature changes K in the opposite direction to raising it.
draft.remember: Only temperature changes K. Heating lowers K for exothermic reactions and raises it for endothermic ones.

a.q: The value of K for an exothermic reaction is measured at 300 K. Which change would give a different value of K?
a.why: Only a change in temperature changes K. Adding or removing a substance, or changing pressure, can move the position of equilibrium, but K stays the same at 300 K.
a.clue: Which change affects K itself, not just the amounts present?

b.q: The reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) is exothermic. A plant in Newcastle raises the temperature of its reaction vessel. What happens to K, and why?
opts: K decreases, because the forward reaction releases heat
K increases, because the mixture has more energy
K decreases, because the pressure in the vessel has risen
K stays the same, because equilibrium has been reached
b.why: Raising the temperature lowers K for an exothermic reaction, so less product is present at the new equilibrium. Extra energy does not raise K here, because the forward reaction releases heat rather than absorbs it.
b.clue: Check whether the forward reaction releases or absorbs heat.

b.best: K decreases, because the forward reaction releases heat
